title: Flu Season

jokes.text: Opening narration: 'There is a crazy flu going around. Lots of miserable, dehydrated people with high fevers and diarrhea.'
jokes.setup: Standard sitcom setup for a 'someone is sick' episode — expected to be played relatively straight.
jokes.punchline: The sudden inclusion of 'diarrhea' in an otherwise clinical-sounding list undercuts the professional tone for a cheap-but-effective gross-out laugh.
jokes.explanation: A functional cold-open laugh — the word 'diarrhea' does the work. Leslie's talking-head delivery grounds it in character but the joke is mostly just the unexpected gross word landing in a formal list. Competent but not elevated.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, because nurses have the same training as janitors. That's why there are so many sexy janitor costumes at Halloween.

jokes.text: 'I want another nurse.' / 'Well, there are none. We're stretched pretty thin right now.' / 'Then, I want a janitor. They can do what you do, right?' / 'Yep. Nurses and janitors are totally interchangeable.'
jokes.setup: April, sick and petulant, asks for a different nurse; when told there are none, she requests a janitor instead.
jokes.punchline: Ann's deadpan sarcastic agreement — 'Yep. Nurses and janitors are totally interchangeable' — is perfect professional-grade exasperation from someone who knows she's being insulted but won't give April the satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: Works because both characters are behaving in perfectly consistent ways: April is maximally awful and petulant, and Ann refuses to show she's hurt while clearly being wounded. The escalation from 'different nurse' to 'a janitor' is a great comedic step, and Ann's flat agreement is more cutting than any protest would be.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm too sick to be vindictive right now.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: *buzzing sound of her using a motorized scooter to run over someone's foot*

jokes.text: 'Except no one dresses up like a janitor when they want to be slutty.'
jokes.setup: Ann has sarcastically agreed that nurses and janitors are interchangeable.
jokes.punchline: April twists the knife by pointing out the cultural nurse-costume trope, implying Ann's job is valued primarily as a sexual fantasy — a genuinely mean and very funny observation.
jokes.explanation: This is a standout line. It's perfectly constructed: short, venomous, logical (it follows from the nurse/janitor interchangeability premise), and could ONLY come from April. It takes a mean-spirited observation and packages it with an unexpected cultural reference that makes it feel like sharp wit rather than just cruelty. Highly quotable. This is the episode's first great joke.

dialogue.line: I cannot reliably identify the speaker(s) for this joke. 'JJ' is not a main character in Parks and Recreation, and the punchline description is too vague to reconstruct specific dialogue without the actual text. Please provide the full joke text.

jokes.text: 'Please don't do that.' / 'Do? I can't do anything. I'm sick.' — April's passive-aggressive weaponization of her illness.
jokes.setup: Ann asks April not to take her anger out on her; April has just been doing exactly that.
jokes.punchline: April weaponizes her sick status as a defense — 'I can't do anything, I'm sick' — while having just done quite a lot.
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat — April's refusal to acknowledge her own behavior while hiding behind her illness is very on-brand. The irony is clear and lands well, though it's not as sharp as the janitor/slutty nurse line that preceded it.

dialogue.speaker: JJ
dialogue.line: You're right, I do say that to everyone. But the statistics don't lie — you're the only one who's ever bought a whole case of whipped cream at 3 AM, returned it unopened the next morning, and then came back to buy it again two weeks later.

jokes.text: April buzzes the nurse call button repeatedly from her hospital bed — a visual/reaction beat of passive-aggressive harassment.
jokes.setup: April is trapped in a hospital bed and has just told Ann she's powerless because she's sick.
jokes.punchline: She immediately starts buzzing the call button incessantly, proving the opposite — she has full capacity to be a nuisance.
jokes.explanation: A perfect silent callback to her just-delivered claim of helplessness. Purely visual comedy that demonstrates character rather than explains it. The rewatch bonus is earned because the staging makes it funnier on repeat viewings when you know April's personality.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not good at hospital visits. I don't know what to say to people who are sick.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: So I usually just bring them a get-well gift.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Last time I visited someone in the hospital, I brought them a bottle of scotch and a bottle of bacon grease.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I thought, 'Well, if they're stuck in bed, they might as well enjoy the two best things in life.'

jokes.text: Leslie denying she's sick while clearly symptomatic: 'I'm feeling really tired. I think maybe my allergies are acting up. I've already vomited, like, five times today.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is pitching the Harvest Festival to JJ while visibly ill, insisting it's 'just allergies.'
jokes.punchline: She lists 'vomiting five times today' as a symptom consistent with allergies — a deeply illogical equation that reveals her self-denial.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie Knope — her inability to admit weakness or slow down is so deeply ingrained that she genuinely seems to believe vomiting could be an allergy symptom. The joke works because it's absolutely consistent with her character and the logic is internally coherent to Leslie, if no one else.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no political beliefs. And, by the way, I don't care about people.

jokes.text: 'I bet you say that to all the girls.' / 'Oh, no. No, actually, you're my favorite. You spent over $1,000 last year on waffles alone.'
jokes.setup: JJ says Leslie is his favorite customer; Leslie makes a coy, flirtatious joke assuming it's a platitude.
jokes.punchline: JJ reveals it's literally true and documentable — Leslie spent over $1,000 on waffles at his diner in a single year.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully efficient joke that does double duty: it's funny as a pure punchline AND it deepens our understanding of Leslie Knope's iconic waffle obsession by giving it a concrete (and absurd) dollar figure. The misdirection from romantic platitude to accounting fact is well-executed. Strong character integration — this joke is impossible without Leslie's established personality.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have been working with this man for years, and I still don't know his name. Every time I almost learn it, something happens and I have to start all over again.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: At this point, asking would be admitting I don't know. So we have this unspoken agreement: I pretend to know him, he pretends I know him, and we both go about our business.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's actually the most honest friendship I have.

jokes.text: 'I didn't know what to bring you, so I just got some magazines and lipstick. Woman stuff.'
jokes.setup: Tom visits April in the hospital and brings a gift.
jokes.punchline: 'Woman stuff' — his breezy, reductive categorization of his gift reveals his complete inability to engage with sick people on any emotional level, while also being a hilariously bad gift-giver.
jokes.explanation: Tom at his most Tom — the gift is useless, the reasoning is sexist but oblivious rather than malicious, and 'woman stuff' as the final label is perfectly economical. Works well as a quick character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm tired and sweaty because I've been working hard. You look like that on your best day.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head: 'I'm not very good at visiting people in hospitals, so I'm going to go.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just delivered a bad gift and is clearly uncomfortable.
jokes.punchline: He states his inadequacy as fact and announces his immediate departure with complete self-awareness but zero self-improvement.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the logical gap — most people would apologize or try harder. Tom just acknowledges the problem and leaves. His self-awareness without behavioral change is a well-worn character note but executed with good economy here.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: How was your run?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I did a mile in 4 minutes and 23 seconds.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, that's incredible!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I know. I'm disappointed. My goal was 4:20.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head: 'I'm not interested in caring about people. I once worked with a guy for three years and never learned his name. Best friend I ever had. We still never talk sometimes.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains his philosophy of not caring about people.
jokes.punchline: The triple escalation: never learned his name → best friend I ever had → 'we still never talk sometimes' (a grammatically impossible but emotionally coherent statement).
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. 'We still never talk sometimes' is a grammatically paradoxical sentence that somehow perfectly encapsulates Tom's emotional avoidance — 'never talk sometimes' implies a relationship so distant that its absence is intermittent. It's absurdist logic that makes total emotional sense for the character. The escalating structure (three beats, each more absurd) is beautifully constructed. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: My mile time was slow, but that's only because I was running into a headwind. And the track was slightly uphill. And I hadn't eaten in six hours. And I was wearing jeans.

jokes.text: 'You look tired and you're all sweaty.' / 'You look tired and you're all sweaty all the time. What's your excuse?'
jokes.setup: Jerry points out that Leslie looks unwell.
jokes.punchline: Leslie turns the observation back on Jerry by pointing out he ALWAYS looks that way, implying her symptoms are actually his baseline state.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient Jerry burn that works because it simultaneously reveals Leslie's denial (she's using Jerry's appearance as proof she's fine) while landing a classic Jerry diss. The structure is clean — setup, mirror, escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, my body is more like a microwave that someone dropped down the stairs.

jokes.text: Leslie bursts through the barricaded door and starts touching everyone's stuff while they recoil in horror. 'She's germing up all my stuff.'
jokes.setup: The team has been preventing Leslie from entering; she forces her way in.
jokes.punchline: Tom's horrified 'She's germing up all my stuff' captures the absurdity — it's less about health concern and more about Tom's precious belongings being contaminated.
jokes.explanation: Tom's possessive horror ('my stuff') is perfectly Tom. The physical comedy of the breach is inferred but clearly funnier on screen. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I literally cannot find a single flaw in Chris. He's perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Which is weird because usually I can find something wrong with everyone. But with Chris, there's nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Except... he won't let me organize his sock drawer. He says it's 'fine as is.'

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: And honestly? That might be the hottest thing he does.

jokes.text: Chris's talking-head about flu prevention: 'My body is finely-tuned, like a microchip, and the flu is like a grain of sand. It could literally shut down the entire system.' / 'My body's like a chip, too. A potato chip.'
jokes.setup: Chris explains his obsessive fitness philosophy using the microchip/grain of sand metaphor.
jokes.punchline: Ann's deflating self-comparison: 'A potato chip.' — simultaneously self-deprecating, relatable, and a perfect puncturing of Chris's grandiosity.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect two-line joke. Chris's metaphor is already funny in its self-important precision, but Ann's 'potato chip' response is the ideal comic deflation — it uses the same metaphorical frame, delivers complete self-awareness, and is irresistibly quotable. The economy is exceptional: two words ('potato chip') do the work of a paragraph. This is the kind of joke that gets repeated.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I need someone to replace April. Someone who's mean, apathetic, has no respect for authority, and actively works against the department's interests.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So you're looking for another April?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No. I'm looking for someone with all of those qualities, plus they have to be good at their job. April was the whole package.

jokes.text: 'Speaking of potato chips, you and I are on for dinner tomorrow, yes?'
jokes.setup: Ann has just compared herself to a potato chip; Chris enthusiastically pivots to confirming their date.
jokes.punchline: The 'speaking of potato chips' transition is absurdly smooth — Chris uses the food metaphor as a social bridge with characteristic oblivious confidence, also implying he may have genuinely enjoyed the potato chip metaphor.
jokes.explanation: A smooth callback that works because Chris's social obliviousness is perfectly rendered — he uses 'speaking of potato chips' as a genuine conversational transition, which is both charming and absurd. The joke rewards attention.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, I have something new to show you guys.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I call it... the Mega Straw. It's just straws taped together.

jokes.text: Ann's talking-head about Chris: 'The problem is he's like a perfect human man. I can't find one flaw. There was one time I thought he farted. But it was me.'
jokes.setup: Ann gushes about how perfect Chris is and her inability to find any flaw in him.
jokes.punchline: 'There was one time I thought he farted. But it was me.' — the anti-climactic reveal that the one 'flaw' she found wasn't even his undermines her entire search for imperfection.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely excellent joke. The structure is flawless: you're set up for a revelation about Chris's flaw, then you get the fart story (already funny), then the second beat ('but it was me') completely deflates the story and reveals Ann's own embarrassing misattribution. The self-own makes it better than a simple gross-out gag. Extremely quotable. One of the episode's standout moments.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're sick? But you're so healthy and strong. I've never seen you vulnerable before. It's actually kind of... attractive? No, wait, that's wrong. I mean, I'm concerned about your wellbeing as a colleague and friend.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'I need to find someone to fill in for April. Now, I know I'm not going to find someone who's both aggressively mean and apathetic. April really is the whole package.'
jokes.setup: Ron needs a temp replacement for April, who is sick.
jokes.punchline: He describes April's 'whole package' as being 'aggressively mean and apathetic' — framing her worst qualities as professional virtues in Ron's specific value system.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Ron's worldview is so thoroughly anti-government and pro-inefficiency that he genuinely prizes April's hostility to work. 'The whole package' is the perfect phrase because it's what you'd say about an ideal employee — Ron just inverts what 'ideal' means. High character integration score because this joke is entirely dependent on Ron's unique value system.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes! A microchip! That's exactly what I was going to say. We need to think of Pawnee as a microchip, and each department is like a tiny transistor, and if one transistor fails, the whole microchip... wait, what does a microchip do?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It processes information.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right, right. So we need to process information better. As a microchip.

jokes.text: Andy's 'Super-straw' invention: a comically oversized straw he presents to Ron with pride.
jokes.setup: Ron asks Andy to fill in as his assistant; Andy cheerfully shows up and immediately shows off an 'invention.'
jokes.punchline: The 'Super-straw' — implied to be a regular straw or an absurdly large one — presented with the full enthusiasm of someone who believes they've innovated.
jokes.explanation: Andy's child-like enthusiasm for something trivial is perfectly in character. The joke relies heavily on the visual of whatever the Super-straw actually is, which the transcript can't fully convey. Works as a quick Andy moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have a very important meeting with the city council about the Ramsett Park expansion project.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've been preparing for weeks, going over all the details, making sure everything is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is basically like when Harry Potter had to prepare for the Triwizard Tournament.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean, not Harry Potter. I don't know why I said that. I have a fever.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is like when I had to prepare to become Deputy Director.

jokes.text: 'Do I have to tuck my shirt in? Because, honestly, that's kind of a deal breaker.'
jokes.setup: Ron has hired Andy to fill in as his assistant and is explaining the job.
jokes.punchline: Andy treats tucking in his shirt as a non-negotiable dealbreaker for an office job — inverting normal employment logic where the employer sets conditions.
jokes.explanation: Andy's priorities are completely inverted — he treats comfort as more important than employment — but he delivers it with such genuine earnestness that it's hard to dislike. Well-executed character joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so what are your symptoms?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I've been feeling dizzy and nauseous all morning.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hmm, let me see... Have you tried turning it off and turning it back on again?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? That's not medical advice.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No wait, wait. I got it. You have a fatal error. You need to restart your system immediately.

jokes.text: Leslie insisting she's not sick while describing a clearly illness-based Claritin chain: 'I took a Claritin and I threw that up, so I took another one. I threw that up. And then, I took a third and it stayed down. I'm getting better.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is confronting Leslie about being sick; she insists it's allergies.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm getting better' — her triumphant conclusion after describing a sequence that constitutes a medical emergency of its own, with the word 'better' being absurdly inappropriate.
jokes.explanation: The three-beat escalation (threw up, threw up, stayed down) followed by 'I'm getting better' is beautifully constructed. Each beat is worse than the last, and the conclusion that this constitutes improvement is the perfect payoff. Leslie's unshakeable optimism in the face of physical disaster is her defining trait at its most comedic. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not sick, see? I can do a cartwheel!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What are you doing?

jokes.text: 'I have to get ready for the Chamber of Secrets.' / 'Commerce.'
jokes.setup: Leslie, feverish, is arguing that she needs to get to the Chamber of Commerce meeting.
jokes.punchline: She calls it the 'Chamber of Secrets' (the Harry Potter location), and Ben's flat correction — 'Commerce' — serves as both the punchline and the straight-man reaction.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly economical joke — the substitution of 'Secrets' for 'Commerce' is funny both as a fever-brain slip and as an unexpected pop culture reference. Ben's single-word correction as punchline is exactly the right move. The joke is short, sharp, and gets maximum mileage from minimum words.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm just worried that Ben might not be ready for this presentation. He's been working so hard, but what if he freezes up? What if he forgets his talking points? What if he gets a fever and forgets who he is?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I'll be fine. It's just a presentation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's what you said before the Harvest Festival, and you ended up with heat exhaustion.

jokes.text: 'Leslie, I typed your symptoms into the thing up here, and it says you could have network connectivity problems.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is clearly very sick; Tom is trying to help by looking up her symptoms.
jokes.punchline: Tom has apparently typed symptoms into a computer and received a diagnosis of 'network connectivity problems' — a tech error message he's interpreted as medical information.
jokes.explanation: An absurdist gem. Tom's attempt at helpfulness results in him reading a computer error as a medical diagnosis, which he delivers with complete sincerity. It works on multiple levels: it's a realistic tech fail, it reveals Tom's limited competence, and 'network connectivity problems' as a medical diagnosis is genuinely surreal. 'The thing up here' is also funny in its vagueness.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm going to the spa. Arrivaderci!

jokes.text: Leslie protests she's not sick by attempting cartwheels: 'If I was sick, could I do this?' — then clearly fails at performing them.
jokes.setup: Ann has taken Leslie's temperature (104.1) and tells her she's dehydrated and needs to be admitted.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's cartwheel challenge — and Ann's flat 'No' when asked if she's doing them — reveals her complete physical incapacity while she remains convinced she's fine.
jokes.explanation: Strong physical comedy moment — the image of Leslie in professional attire attempting cartwheels to prove she's healthy is inherently funny. Ann's deadpan 'No' is perfectly calibrated. The visual is implied and presumably very funny on screen. Rewatch bonus for the physical performance.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey there! Welcome to Parks and Rec. I'm Andy, I'm the receptionist now.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So what can I do you for? Wait, that's not right. What can I do for you?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, I don't know where anything is. Or who anyone is. Is this the Parks Department or the... um... Rec Department?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what, let me transfer you to someone who might know what they're doing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: How do I do that? Do I just yell into the phone?

jokes.text: Ben's talking-head: 'It's not that I don't trust Ben. It's that I don't have faith in Ben. And, also, I'm starting to forget who Ben is.'
jokes.setup: Leslie (feverish) is explaining why she doesn't trust Ben to handle the meeting.
jokes.punchline: The three-beat escalation from 'don't trust' to 'no faith' to 'forgetting who he is' reveals her fever is affecting her cognition while she still insists she's fine enough to work.
jokes.explanation: A great escalating joke. The first two beats ('don't trust,' 'no faith') are character-consistent, but the third — 'I'm starting to forget who Ben is' — is the surprise that reveals her brain is actively deteriorating. The fact that she's doing this talking-head ABOUT Ben while forgetting him makes it funnier. Clean three-step structure with a genuine punch at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I brought you some fresh pillows.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why would you do this? What did I ever do to you?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Are you trying to kill me? Is this poisoned?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I trusted you, Ann. I thought we were friends.

jokes.text: Tom explains his preparation strategy to Ben: 'The worst thing you can do with an important presentation like this is over-prepare. So, I think it's best if I go to the spa.'
jokes.setup: Ben expects Tom to help him prepare for the Chamber of Commerce meeting, as they promised Leslie.
jokes.punchline: Tom presents going to the spa as anti-over-preparation, reframing laziness as strategy — and then adds 'Arrivederci' as a final flourish.
jokes.explanation: Tom's genius for rationalizing laziness is on full display. The inversion of 'over-prepare = bad, spa = good' is silly but consistent with who Tom is. 'Arrivederci' as an exit line is a nice Tom flourish.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm going to maintain professionalism and keep my emotions in check.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I've been stress testing a new technique where I imagine Ron's face on a punching bag, then I actually punch a real bag, but I'm picturing his face.

jokes.text: 'See, I never promise Leslie anything. That way, I never disappoint her. I try to be considerate.'
jokes.setup: Ben points out they promised Leslie they'd prep for the meeting.
jokes.punchline: Tom frames never making promises as a form of consideration — redefining self-serving behavior as thoughtfulness with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Tom's ethical inversions are a reliable comic engine, and this one is well-constructed. The logic is airtight from Tom's perspective, which makes it funnier than a straightforward excuse. 'I try to be considerate' as the conclusion is the right note of oblivious self-congratulation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I could write you a rap for your presentation!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, no. That's a terrible idea. I'm not a rapper.

jokes.text: Andy answering Ron's phone: 'Ron Swanson's office.' — then immediately transferring to a dial tone.
jokes.setup: Andy has been hired as Ron's temporary receptionist and is sitting at the desk.
jokes.punchline: Andy answers the phone professionally then immediately drops the call — framed as 'I just dropped another call,' implying this is a pattern.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient joke about Andy's incompetence. The deadpan delivery of 'I just dropped another call' implies plural failures without needing to show them. Well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm hungry.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I haven't eaten since breakfast. I'm basically starving to death.

jokes.text: April accuses Ann of trying to smother her: 'Are you trying to smother me? Help! This slutty nurse is trying to smother me to death with a pillow!'
jokes.setup: Ann brings April a fresh set of pillows as a kind gesture.
jokes.punchline: April interprets the kindness as an assassination attempt and shouts 'slutty nurse' — a callback to her earlier insult — while calling for help as though Ann is a genuine threat.
jokes.explanation: A good escalation of the April-Ann antagonism. April's paranoia is perfectly calibrated and the callback to 'slutty nurse' rewards viewers who remember the earlier insult. The willingness to call for help from a hospital that Ann works in is a nice added layer of absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You gotta try the Meat Tornado. It's amazing. A guy died eating one last year, but that's just because he didn't appreciate it enough.

jokes.text: Ann's talking-head: 'I know what she's trying to do. She's trying to get me to break. And you know what? I'm not going to do it. I'm going to be professional and I'm going to put on a happy face. And then, I'm going to go into a supply closet and snap a bunch of tongue depressors.'
jokes.setup: Ann has been nursing a hostile April and is trying to maintain professionalism.
jokes.punchline: The pivot to 'I'm going to go into a supply closet and snap a bunch of tongue depressors' is the specific, slightly unhinged coping mechanism that makes it funny — it's petty, it's very specific, and it's clearly something Ann has planned.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Ann's plan is so specific and so petty — tongue depressors are cheap and plentiful in a hospital, so snapping them is pure cathartic theater with no real consequence. The phrase 'snap a bunch of tongue depressors' is perfectly chosen for maximum absurdity. Ann's maintaining-dignity-while-planning-petty-revenge is a relatable and well-written beat.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's called the Pit. It comes in a bag. You eat it with a shovel.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm in.

jokes.text: 'Do you want me to write you a rap? I'll write you a rap.' / 'No, you know what? You're never going to be able to pull it off. You're too white.'
jokes.setup: Delirious Leslie is trying to help Ben prepare for the presentation, offering to write him a rap.
jokes.punchline: She immediately talks herself out of it by concluding he's 'too white' — revealing that she has already mentally cast and rejected him in approximately two seconds.
jokes.explanation: A quick, funny beat from delirious Leslie. The joke is in the speed — she offers and rejects the idea in the same breath. 'You're too white' is a bit of an easy punchline but it's delivered well in context. The fever logic that a rap is even on the table is the better joke.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A spa is like a kitchen, right? You got your chef, that's me. You got your sous chefs, that's you guys. And you got your ingredients. But here's the thing - I'm not gonna use the word 'ingredients' because that's a little too close to how people used to talk about, you know, other people. So let's call them 'components.' I'm the chef, you're my sous chefs, and this spa experience is the dish we're cooking up together.

jokes.text: 'I have some great news. I think my fever just broke.' — said immediately before Ben cuts the conversation off and leaves.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been clearly feverish and delirious throughout the scene.
jokes.punchline: She announces her fever has broken with total confidence and optimism — the joke being that she has no basis for this claim whatsoever and her subsequent behavior will prove otherwise.
jokes.explanation: A nice character beat that sustains the running gag of Leslie's denial, but it's a middle-of-pack execution. Works well as a button on the scene.

jokes.text: Ron orders the 'Meat Tornado' burrito after Andy describes it as having 'literally killed a guy last year.' 'You had me at Meat Tornado.'
jokes.setup: Andy recommends Big Head Joe's burritos and mentions one called the 'Meat Tornado' that 'literally killed a guy last year.'
jokes.punchline: 'You had me at Meat Tornado' — Ron's enthusiastic endorsement of a food item that recently killed someone is entirely consistent with his carnivore philosophy and distrust of safety-focused thinking.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. 'Meat Tornado' is a name so perfectly calibrated for Ron Swanson that it almost feels like it was invented for him. 'You had me at Meat Tornado' riffs on the 'You had me at hello' rom-com line in a way that is perfectly character-specific. The dark humor of enthusiastically ordering something that killed a person is quintessential Ron. High originality, perfect character integration, very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey Ann, are you okay? You look sick.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, I mean you actually look sick. I'm not trying to flirt with you or anything. When I say 'fine,' I mean actually fine, not the thing where guys say a girl is fine.

jokes.text: Leslie has escaped the hospital, is wearing a scarf, and asks Ben: 'Does this scarf look okay? I don't want to look stuffy. But I also don't want to look too schlubby.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has stolen flu medicine and escaped the hospital while running a 104-degree fever to attend a business meeting.
jokes.punchline: Her concern is not her health or the medical escape but whether her scarf strikes the right professional register — 'stuffy' vs. 'schlubby.'
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat — Leslie's priorities are so inverted that professional appearance is her primary concern even in medical crisis. 'Stuffy vs. schlubby' is a fun word choice. Not exceptional but very consistent.

jokes.text: Leslie sneaks out of hospital in a scarf, asking if it looks 'stuffy' or too 'schlubby', while being ordered back to bed.
jokes.setup: Ann told Leslie she has to stay in the hospital. Leslie is now trying to leave.
jokes.punchline: The comedy is Leslie's priorities — she's concerned about her presentation appearance (the scarf debate) rather than her 104-degree fever.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's sense of priority is funny — she's weighing scarf aesthetics while gravely ill. 'Schlubby' is a good word choice. The scene works as part of the arc but isn't exceptional standalone.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Did you know that in 1987, the Denver Broncos had the best defense in the NFL? Forty-four sacks in a single season. Forty-four! That's like... that's like one sack for every... *coughs* ...I don't know, math is hard when you're sick. But the point is, John Elway threw for 3,198 yards that year, which is less than I thought, but more than I have fingers and toes combined. Also, the average NFL player makes $1.9 million a year, but that was in 2010, so now it's probably more, or less, depending on inflation and other economic factors that I'm too feverish to understand right now.

jokes.text: Tom's 'Would You Rather' game at the spa: 'Now, what superpower would you rather have? Would you rather be able to fly or be invisible?' / 'Fly, I guess.' / 'I forgot to tell you. You can only fly five feet above the ground.'
jokes.setup: Tom is playing 'Would You Rather' with a group of older spa-goers.
jokes.punchline: After the man chooses 'fly,' Tom retroactively adds the condition that you can only fly five feet off the ground — effectively making the ability useless and completely undermining the choice.
jokes.explanation: Tom's 'Would You Rather' game is a well-structured comedic bit — the late addition of crippling conditions to the superpowers is a classic game that Tom plays with genuine delight. 'Five feet above the ground' is specific enough to be funny without being too absurd. The rhythm of the joke is good: choice, then reveal of the hidden condition.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We should run some pass plays after we eat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's the best idea you've ever had.

jokes.text: Tom's 'Would You Rather': 'Would you rather live in the pocket of a giant kangaroo or have a pocket on your own stomach that has a tiny kangaroo in it all the time?' / 'Tiny kangaroo in my stomach pocket.' / 'Forgot to mention, the tiny kangaroo is a racist.'
jokes.setup: The kangaroo Would You Rather, with its already absurd premise of giant vs. tiny kangaroo scenarios.
jokes.punchline: 'Forgot to mention, the tiny kangaroo is a racist' — the added condition is so unexpected and specific that it reframes the entire premise. A racist kangaroo is a delightfully absurd complication.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's funniest joke. The callback structure builds on the previous 'Would You Rather' condition (flying five feet) and then completely blows past it with an absurdist escalation that nobody could anticipate. 'The tiny kangaroo is a racist' is one of those perfect sentences that is incomprehensible and yet completely clear in what it means for your quality of life. The specificity of 'a racist' (not violent, not loud — a RACIST) is the brilliant choice. This reaches close to an 8.5+ anchor in quality and stands out even in a strong episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Andy's the only one of you idiots who actually knows how to do anything. Ben's too uptight. Jerry's too stupid. Tom's too greedy. And Leslie... well, Leslie's a woman.

jokes.text: Chris's rapid deterioration — he's in the hospital hours after proudly proclaiming his body is like a microchip: 'Things happen very quickly. Listen to me. My brain is on fire. I'm dying.'
jokes.setup: Chris earlier boasted his body was a finely-tuned microchip that a grain of sand could destroy.
jokes.punchline: He's now in the hospital in apparent crisis, having collapsed at a speed consistent with his own prediction — the extreme fragility of his body is now on full display.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff to Chris's earlier boasting. His prediction ('a grain of sand could destroy it') has come true with alarming speed, which validates his self-knowledge while also making his fragility absurdly literal. 'My brain is on fire. I'm dying.' is delivered with Chris's characteristic earnestness.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I need more flu medicine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I already gave you the whole bottle.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, and you drank half of it.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Not like, "Damn, you're fine," but fine health-wise.'
jokes.setup: Chris tells Ann he saw her a few hours ago and she was 'fine'
jokes.punchline: He immediately clarifies 'not like "Damn, you're fine"' — meaning he felt compelled to specify he wasn't complimenting her attractiveness, which paradoxically makes it seem like he was thinking it
jokes.explanation: A lovely piece of character comedy — Chris is so earnest and so aware of his own attractiveness/Ann-attraction that he over-clarifies in a way that reveals more than he intended. The 'Damn, you're fine' self-correction is very Chris Traeger: precise, health-obsessed, and inadvertently flirtatious.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Leslie came to my house last night. It was like a dream.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: April, that literally was a dream. You were asleep.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, it was real. She came through a hole in the wall.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's your closet door, April.

jokes.text: 'The microchip has been compromised. Pierre Garcon was a sixth-round pick. Collie was the fourth round. Indianapolis Colts know how to draft so well.'
jokes.setup: Chris has just declared 'my brain is on fire, I'm dying' in the hospital.
jokes.punchline: His fever-brain pivot to a detailed, accurate analysis of Indianapolis Colts draft picks is a non-sequitur that reveals the specific contents of his feverish mind — the microchip metaphor being 'compromised' is now visualized.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it's specific — not random sports stats, but Colts draft picks specifically, which ties to Pawnee being an Indiana city. The contrast between 'I'm dying' and an organized sports analysis is the comedic mechanism. Chris's fitness obsession extending to encyclopedic sports knowledge is believable character detail.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, can you lend me some cab money?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Sure, here you go.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thanks. I'm running a fever and I'm seeing hieroglyphics on the taxi meter.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'I like Andy. I'm surrounded by a lot of women in this department. And that includes the men.'
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining why he enjoys having Andy around.
jokes.punchline: 'And that includes the men' — Ron's assessment of his male colleagues' masculinity, delivered as a simple statement of fact rather than an insult, is a classic Swanson deadpan.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Ron Swanson line — it's delivered without heat, it's not even clearly meant as an insult (from Ron's perspective it might just be accurate information), and the character integration is exceptionally high. Only Ron Swanson would assess the masculinity of his male coworkers so clinically and share it so casually. The economy is elite: the entire joke is six words.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Be careful walking down those stairs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Don't worry, I'm great at spatial reasoning. I can walk down stairs forwards, backwards, sideways. I once walked down a flight of stairs while doing a cartwheel.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not possible.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I landed on my head, but I did it.

jokes.text: Ron and Andy playing catch in the parking lot — 'Peyton Manning reading the defense! Reggie Wayne, Colts corner!' followed by a car alarm going off.
jokes.setup: Ron's elderly lunch companion suggests they 'run a few pass plays' in the parking lot to burn calories.
jokes.punchline: They actually do it, with Andy doing sports commentary, and a car alarm suggests someone's car was hit — the implied physical comedy of the throw going wild.
jokes.explanation: A fun physical comedy sequence that would play better on screen. The car alarm as the punchline (implying a badly thrown pass hit a car) is a clean visual comedic beat. Andy's enthusiastic play-by-play for what is presumably a terrible game of catch is well-suited to his character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Good morning everyone, I'm Leslie Knope, and welcome to 'The Real Housewives of Pawnee.'

jokes.text: April's talking-head: 'I had a dream that she came into this room, stole my flu medicine, told me not to tell you, and then disappeared through that hole in the wall.' / 'The door?'
jokes.setup: Ann asks if April knows where Leslie is; April needs to not reveal what she knows.
jokes.punchline: April frames her accurate memory of events as 'a dream,' and when Ann corrects 'hole in the wall' to 'the door,' it underlines that April is describing real events as fictional with a straight face.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully executed joke. April's alibi is to frame factual events as a 'dream,' but she includes the detail of 'a hole in the wall' — a telling slip that reveals she was actually conscious. Ann's correction ('the door?') is the perfect understated punchline that confirms the audience's suspicion without overplaying it. April's absolutely straight face makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, I got that right? I didn't even study!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I just assumed all the answers were 'America' and one of them had to be correct.

jokes.text: April tells Andy's stand-in (nurse): 'I didn't take any [flu medicine]. Leslie came in here and stole it and left.'
jokes.setup: The nurse checks in on April, who asked for more flu medicine.
jokes.punchline: It's revealed that Leslie — the woman who insists she's fine — broke into the hospital room and stole April's flu medicine.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Leslie stole April's flu medicine is a great story beat that doubles as comedy — it explains how Leslie powered through the meeting and confirms her pathological drive. The escalation of Leslie's desperation to this point is genuinely funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm so excited about this business opportunity. I might have thrown up a little in my mouth just now, but I'm not sure if it was in my mouth or on the table.

jokes.text: Ben encounters fever-Leslie at the Chamber of Commerce: 'I looked at the meter, and it had Egyptian hieroglyphics on it.' / 'Do you know the exchange rate?'
jokes.setup: Leslie has escaped the hospital and taken a cab; Ben asks how much the fare was.
jokes.punchline: Leslie describes the taxi meter as displaying Egyptian hieroglyphics (her feverish misreading of numbers), and Ben's completely earnest follow-up — 'Do you know the exchange rate?' — treats the absurdity as logistically solvable.
jokes.explanation: An excellent two-line exchange. Leslie's fever-hallucination of hieroglyphics on the meter is a vivid comedic image, but Ben's response ('Do you know the exchange rate?') is what makes it exceptional — he accepts the premise entirely and tries to solve it practically, which is both funny and perfectly in character for Ben, who is earnestly problem-oriented even in absurd situations.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Kidneys, you're on notice. Liver, you're next.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Be careful.' / Ben: 'What?' / Leslie: 'The floor and the wall just switched.'
jokes.setup: Ben is navigating the Chamber of Commerce venue with a very sick Leslie.
jokes.punchline: 'The floor and the wall just switched' — Leslie's hallucination is reported as a helpful spatial warning, with the matter-of-fact delivery making it funnier.
jokes.explanation: A short, very clean joke. Leslie's hallucination is delivered as a helpful navigational tip, which is funnier than if it were reported as a symptom. The economy is excellent — just six words carry the entire comedic payload. 'The floor and the wall just switched' is genuinely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, come on, get up.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't. I'm emotionally attached to this floor now. We've been through so much together.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You've been lying there for twenty minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Exactly. That's a lifetime in floor years.

jokes.text: Leslie's opening line at the Chamber of Commerce: 'Good evening, everyone. I'm Leslie Monster. And this is Nightline.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has insisted on doing the presentation despite running a 104-degree fever; Ben has reluctantly let her take the stage.
jokes.punchline: She introduces herself as 'Leslie Monster' and announces they're on 'Nightline,' apparently hallucinating she's hosting a news program. Ben's quiet 'Okay, I wouldn't open with that' is the perfect reaction.
jokes.explanation: A great fever-brain moment. 'Leslie Monster' is an unexpected name that reveals her reality is fragmenting — she's incorporated her own name but scrambled it. 'And this is Nightline' suggests she believes she's on television. Ben's gentle, understated 'Okay, I wouldn't open with that' is exactly the right reaction — not alarmed, just professionally concerned. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know, being completely incapacitated has really given me time to reflect on the positive aspects of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've realized that I don't have to go to the gym because I literally cannot move.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: And I don't have to meal prep because I can only consume liquids.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: So really, this is the most optimized I've ever been.

jokes.text: Fever-Leslie engages in a mini policy debate: 'Libertarianism is all about individual liberty. And it should never be defined by the terms liberal or conservative.' / 'And communism is no good, right? That's right.' / 'Big swing and a miss.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been guided to a seat and is in a fever state.
jokes.punchline: She spontaneously begins delivering what sounds like a political science lecture, then pivots to 'communism is no good' (with herself agreeing), and Ben's 'big swing and a miss' narrates the absurdity without quite stopping it.
jokes.explanation: Good fever-delirium comedy — Leslie's brain is accessing civics knowledge and mixing it with the present situation. 'And communism is no good, right? That's right' (talking to herself) is the funniest part. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you can't present this to the council.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, come on, Ben! Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Because it's not ready. We need more time.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Listen here, Seamus, I'm presenting this today.

jokes.text: Leslie's fever-brain quiz: 'And what's the word for when a few clerics are in charge?' / 'Religious oligarchy.' / 'Holy (BLEEP). I can remember things.'
jokes.setup: Ben has been trying to manage delirious Leslie; she spontaneously quizzes him on political science.
jokes.punchline: When Ben correctly answers 'religious oligarchy,' Leslie reacts with genuine astonishment — 'Holy (BLEEP). I can remember things' — as if her own memory is a surprise to her.
jokes.explanation: The surprise is the inversion — it's Ben who answers correctly, and Leslie who is amazed that SHE can remember things (not him). Her fever-brain doesn't quite process that he answered; she takes credit for the knowledge. 'Holy (bleep). I can remember things.' is a good confused-delighted reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, I have a very important presentation about the budget crisis, but first I want to tell you about this amazing deal I just got on a leather briefcase. It's half off at Nordstrom. Half off! Do you know what this means? It means I'm basically making money by buying it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, that's not right. Let me think about this math again. Actually, I think I need to buy two briefcases now. I'm going to run down to Nordstrom real quick.

jokes.text: 'I vomited somewhere in this room. I don't remember where, though.' / 'Wait. You might want to check that drawer.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie are in the Chamber of Commerce room before the meeting.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has vomited in a drawer and doesn't know which one — Ben's 'you might want to check that drawer' implies he's identified the correct one, perhaps by smell.
jokes.explanation: A good gross-out joke elevated by Ben's deadpan. The implication of how he identifies the correct drawer (smell, presumably) is left unspoken, which is the right choice. 'Wait. You might want to check that drawer.' is perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: April, you've been really rude to me all week.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not true. I've been professional. It's not my fault you can't tell the difference between professional April and personal April.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What's the difference?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Professional April wouldn't say this, but personal April thinks you're an idiot.

jokes.text: 'Stop pooping.'
jokes.setup: Ben is managing Leslie in a feverish state in a public venue before a major business meeting.
jokes.punchline: The line 'Stop pooping' — spoken with presumably the same calm tone Ben uses for everything — implies Leslie is actively having a bathroom-related incident and Ben's only recourse is a verbal request.
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum impact. 'Stop pooping' as a professional instruction from a government budget manager to his colleague in a business meeting venue is a surreal comedic image. The economy is perfect — two words and you've got the whole picture. Its quotability is high because the context is so specific and yet so universal in its exasperated directness.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay, I respect that.

jokes.text: Chris on the hospital floor: 'Nothing like a complete physical breakdown to make a guy seem less intimidating. I love the flu.'
jokes.setup: Chris, who earlier projected extraordinary physical confidence, is now on the hospital floor having a complete breakdown.
jokes.punchline: His observation that the breakdown makes him 'less intimidating' frames the situation through his fitness-as-social-currency worldview — and 'I love the flu' is a bizarre conclusion to reach from the floor of a hospital.
jokes.explanation: Chris's positive reframing of illness ('I love the flu') is consistent with his relentlessly optimistic character. The joke works because of the stark contrast between his earlier boasting and current position on the floor. 'Less intimidating' suggests he sees social intimidation as a baseline condition he's temporarily lost.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That was incredible. You just pulled off the flu game. Michael Jordan played the Finals with the flu. You just presented the Sweetums deal while actually having the flu.

jokes.text: Tom reveals his 'spa buddies' secured 25 vans from their car dealerships for the Harvest Festival — his laziness accidentally became a networking win.
jokes.setup: Ben assumed Tom wasted the day at the spa while he did all the work.
jokes.punchline: Tom's spa day turns out to have generated a major donation to the Harvest Festival — his social instincts accidentally succeeded where preparation would have.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying subversion — Tom's apparent laziness pays off, making him simultaneously wrong in his reasoning and right in his outcome. Good structural storytelling that also functions as a character joke. The comedy is in the premise (accidental success via spa) rather than any particular line.

dialogue.speaker: Business Owner
dialogue.line: So how exactly does the sales tax work?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, it's simple. The sales tax is calculated on the total purchase price, and then... wait, why is your face doing that? Your mouth is getting bigger. Are you a snake? Oh my God, you're a snake person!

jokes.text: Ron subtly tells Andy that April is in the hospital — 'April's in the hospital, sick with the flu.' / Andy: 'What? I knew it! I didn't know that.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been asking Ron about April's absence while pretending not to care.
jokes.punchline: 'What? I knew it! I didn't know that.' — Andy's immediate contradiction of himself in consecutive sentences, with genuine surprise at both the information and his own reaction.
jokes.explanation: Andy's emotional transparency is perfectly captured here — he can't maintain any pretense and immediately contradicts himself in a way that makes logical sense emotionally even if linguistically impossible. 'I knew it! I didn't know that.' is a great Andy line because it's not a joke he's making — it's a sincere reaction that is itself the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I think that covers everything. Thank you all for coming. Before I go, I'd like to introduce our special guest speaker.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Please welcome Ben Wyatt, star of 'Lil' Sebastian: The Reckoning.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was never in that show.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, you are now!

jokes.text: Tom introduces the Harvest Festival presentation with a full advertisement for Ladies' Night at the Snakehole Lounge, deadpanning it as a 'quick announcement.'
jokes.setup: Tom is supposed to introduce Leslie at a formal Chamber of Commerce business meeting.
jokes.punchline: He uses the professional platform to promote his own nightclub (the Snakehole Lounge), framing it as a 'quick announcement' — completely inappropriate self-promotion in a business context.
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom Haverford behavior — using any platform available to promote his own business interests, completely unabashed. The Chamber of Commerce meeting as a vehicle for Snakehole Lounge promotion is perfectly Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I need you to find my tiara. It's very important to me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's just a tiara.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just a tiara? This is the Countess Sparklington's crown of majesty, and I need it post-hence!

jokes.text: 'Oh, no, that can't be right. That's way too good of a deal.' / 'Nope. That is what it says. Wow.'
jokes.setup: Tom is reading the Ladies' Night promotion from his own flyer at the presentation.
jokes.punchline: Tom is apparently surprised by his own promotion — he seems genuinely unsure of the deal he himself created, and 'Wow' at the end suggests even he's impressed/skeptical.
jokes.explanation: Tom being confused by his own promotional material is a good beat but the humor is somewhat soft. Works as an extension of the Snakehole bit.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna stay right here by your side while you sleep. I'm not going anywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? I'm gonna go grab some lunch. I'll be back in like... four hours.

jokes.text: Delirious Leslie walks to the podium and delivers an actually coherent, excellent speech to the Chamber of Commerce despite running a 104 fever.
jokes.setup: Everyone (including Ben) expects Leslie to embarrass herself or collapse during the presentation.
jokes.punchline: She delivers a pitch-perfect, inspirational speech — the joke being that Leslie is so competent that even complete physical incapacity can't stop her professional performance.
jokes.explanation: This is structural comedy — the joke is in the subversion of expectation. All signs pointed to disaster, but Leslie's core competence (and sheer will) overcomes everything. The humor isn't in a line but in the situation. High character integration because this only works for Leslie Knope specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, you're so beautiful when you sleep. Your skin is so soft and your hair smells like... oh my god, what is that smell? Did something die in your mouth? Have you been licking a tire?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But I love you anyway.

jokes.text: Tom's introduction: 'It is now my great honor to welcome to the stage the woman responsible for the entire Harvest Festival. Ladies and gentlemen, Leslie Knope!' [Leslie staggers to the podium, clearly barely alive]
jokes.setup: Tom delivers a grand, professional introduction for Leslie
jokes.punchline: The gap between the heroic introduction and the barely-functioning, flu-ridden person who answers it — the physical comedy of Leslie's appearance vs. the grandeur of Tom's words
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the visual juxtaposition — the big introduction vs. the shambling figure who appears. This is standard but well-executed irony. Impact is higher than craft because Amy Poehler's physical performance sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm going to go for a light run. I'm feeling much better.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Chris, you were just hospitalized with the flu.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Treat yo self.

jokes.text: Tom introduces Leslie to the room as simply 'Leslie Knope' — then there is a long, ominous pause before she appears.
jokes.setup: After the Snakehole Lounge digression, Tom pivots to the main event.
jokes.punchline: A long gap between Tom's introduction and Leslie's appearance — the room presumably watching nothing happen — builds dread about what condition she's going to arrive in.
jokes.explanation: An implied comedy beat — the gap between introduction and Leslie's arrival at the podium must be comedically long given her state. Works better as a visual/tonal beat than on paper.

jokes.text: Ann's speech to April: 'While I was on duty, I didn't. Now it's just me.' — then immediately laying into April after clocking out.
jokes.setup: April has been awful to Ann throughout, and Ann has maintained professionalism. When Ann's shift ends, she makes a declaration.
jokes.punchline: The professional/personal binary is the joke — Ann has been holding it together, and the moment she's off the clock, she becomes a completely different person. The setup of 'I thought you weren't gonna lose it' makes the release even better.
jokes.explanation: A well-earned payoff to the Ann-April tension. The 'on duty' vs. 'just me' distinction is a classic comedic release structure. The fact that Ann's confrontation is righteous and emotionally earned makes it satisfying rather than just funny.

jokes.text: April's talking-head, watching Ann's confrontation: 'That's the most I've ever liked Ann.'
jokes.setup: Ann has just confronted April about her behavior with genuine passion and anger.
jokes.punchline: April's grudging, underplayed respect — 'that's the most I've ever liked Ann' — is a perfect character reaction that requires no setup beyond what we've seen. April responds to aggression, not kindness.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect one-liner. It's eight words, it tells you everything about April's character (she respects confrontation over kindness), it's a grudging compliment that's also a continuing insult (the 'most I've ever liked' implies the baseline is still quite low), and it completely inverts the emotional arc of Ann's speech. The economy is exceptional. This is one of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: Ben's sports metaphors comparing Leslie's speech to 'a flu-ridden Michael Jordan at the '97 NBA Finals' and 'Kirk Gibson hobbling up to the plate and hitting a homer off of Dennis Eckersley' — then: 'That was Leslie Knope.'
jokes.setup: Ben is overwhelmed by Leslie's unexpectedly excellent speech and tries to articulate how impressive it was.
jokes.punchline: He escalates through two legendary sports moments and then lands on 'That was Leslie Knope' — making her the third and culminating legendary achievement, elevated above the historical sports comparisons.
jokes.explanation: A great piece of comedy writing. The joke builds through two genuinely legendary sports moments (Jordan's flu game, Gibson's homer) and then the punchline is a character's name — the implication being that Leslie Knope is in that tier. It's simultaneously a joke about Ben's earnestness and a sincere compliment to Leslie. The structure (three examples, third is the reveal) is classically well-constructed. Reveals something about Ben's character (nerdy sports knowledge + genuine admiration for Leslie).

jokes.text: Post-speech, Leslie is asked about sales-tax incentives and responds: 'That's a very good question, sir, and I would counter with my own question, which is, why is half of your face all swirly?'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just delivered a coherent speech but is still feverish; an audience member asks a legitimate policy question.
jokes.punchline: She validates the question professionally and then counters with a hallucination — the swirly face — framed with the same professional rhetoric as a policy counter-argument.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional construction. The joke works because Leslie uses her professional rhetoric ('that's a very good question, sir, and I would counter with my own question') as scaffolding for a completely deranged hallucination. The contrast between the formal setup and the content of the counter-question is perfectly timed. 'Why is half of your face all swirly?' is a highly specific and very visual hallucination that's both funny in description and character-consistent.

jokes.text: 'Give it up, everybody, for Scott Bakula from Quantum Leap.'
jokes.setup: Ben has stepped in to answer questions while Leslie is clearly losing her grip on reality.
jokes.punchline: Leslie introduces Ben as 'Scott Bakula from Quantum Leap' — a specific, odd pop culture misidentification that reveals her fever brain's particular associations.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Scott Bakula from Quantum Leap' is what makes this work — it's not a generic famous person, it's a very particular 1990s TV actor that somehow Leslie's brain has mapped onto Ben. The 'from Quantum Leap' is the essential qualifying detail. Highly quotable because it's so specific and odd.

jokes.text: 'Was I wearing a tiara when I came in here? Because if you happen upon it, will you have Lady Pennyface retrieve it and send it post-hence?'
jokes.setup: Ben is guiding Leslie out after her speech has been redirected.
jokes.punchline: Leslie asks about a tiara and then asks 'Lady Pennyface' to retrieve it — a completely invented person with an aristocratic but incoherent name, and 'post-hence' is a made-up formal phrase.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best fever-brain moments. 'Lady Pennyface' is an inspired name for a hallucinated person — it sounds formal but is completely nonsensical. 'Post-hence' is a great made-up formal word that sounds like it should exist. The entire request is delivered in the tone of someone giving clear, reasonable instructions, which is perfect. High originality for the specific invented details.

jokes.text: Andy visits April in the hospital, promises to stay by her side, then gives up almost immediately: 'You could be asleep for hours. Maybe I'll come back later.'
jokes.setup: Andy has crept into April's hospital room and whispered his intention to stay by her side no matter what.
jokes.punchline: His resolve lasts approximately 10 seconds before the prospect of waiting becomes too much — 'You could be asleep for hours. Maybe I'll come back later.' — deflating his own heroic gesture.
jokes.explanation: A very well-structured character joke. Andy's grand romantic gesture collapses the moment it meets the reality of waiting. The setup (whispered promises, genuine tenderness) makes the punchline land harder. The character integration is high — only Andy would mean both statements completely sincerely.

jokes.text: Andy's continued monologue to sleeping April: 'And I know you think that I'm a jerk, but I hope you can forgive me. / Gross. Your forehead is all sweaty. That's gross. / But I still like you. Okay. That's disgusting.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to have a genuine, vulnerable moment with the sleeping April.
jokes.punchline: He interrupts his own heartfelt declaration to note that her sweaty forehead is disgusting — twice — and then returns to 'I still like you' as though the grossness was a digression rather than a central observation.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully character-specific. Andy's romantic declaration is genuine, but his inability to filter his disgust at the sweaty forehead — noted twice — and then the recovery ('But I still like you. That's disgusting.') creates a rhythm that is completely Andy. It's sweet AND funny, which is the show's best mode. The interweaving of sincere emotion with unfiltered gross-out reaction is executed perfectly.

jokes.text: Ben and Chris discuss their new assignment; Chris is about to go for 'a light 15k' despite having just been hospitalized.
jokes.setup: Chris was completely incapacitated by the flu hours ago, lying on a hospital floor.
jokes.punchline: He has fully recovered and immediately returns to extreme exercise — a 15k run is framed as 'light' — closing the loop on his fragility/resilience paradox.
jokes.explanation: A good closing callback that bookends Chris's arc — he collapsed with extraordinary speed, and he's recovered with equal speed. 'A light 15k' as his recovery activity is consistent with his character and closes the joke. The episode-level callback earns points but the individual joke is modest.

jokes.text: Final 'Way to go, buddy. Way to go.' — Ben saying it to himself after Chris leaves, mirroring the earlier line Ann said after Chris confirmed their date.
jokes.setup: Earlier in the episode, Ann said 'Way to go, buddy' to herself after successfully confirming a date with Chris.
jokes.punchline: Ben echoes the same phrase at episode's end — the ambiguity of whether he's cheering himself on for getting the extension or simply mirroring the earlier moment creates a small comedic beat.
jokes.explanation: A quiet callback that rewards attentive viewers. The mirroring is likely intentional — both characters are quietly celebrating small personal victories. Not a big laugh but a satisfying structural echo.

tmdb_overview: While planning for the local Harvest Festival, Leslie is struck with the flu and is forced to go to the hospital. Ron and Andy have a day of male bonding, and Tom hits the spa.
insight: Flu season spreads 56 jokes across 22 minutes—Parks' densest episode yet through pure character chaos.
